The cowl and nose bowl are flat blanks too: a box-pleated hood and a frustum, with straight creases throughout.

The dot is the loading case selected in the table. The shaded band is the full CG range across all cases. The orange line is the neutral point: the CG must stay ahead of it, and the dashed gap between them is the static margin, the aircraft's pitch stability.
The fold geometry. Every panel in the 3D model is produced by refolding the DXF flat pattern, and the rib-to-spar pilot holes are coordinated between parts.
The laminate acting as one section
The lips are what let thin laminated sheet act as a spar. Without them a free cap edge buckles at about 26 MPa. With them the cap reaches yield before it buckles.

The local-price estimate takes UK VAT off the UK price, converts it at the day's exchange rate, takes about 20 % off US-made hardware, sheet and the engine kit when buying in the US, then adds the country's typical standard VAT, GST or sales tax. It leaves out import duty and shipping. Treat these as rough guides, not quotes.

Ultimate load (×1.5). Colour is the worse of cap stress against its crippling allowable and web shear against buckling. Beam theory along the span, not a finite-element analysis. Grey parts are not analysed yet.

Why start here: the four stands use every skill the aircraft needs, on parts that don't fly. Get it wrong here, not on a spar. You need the stands anyway: the wings are built and parked on them until step 15.
Windscreen: flat sheet, bedded on foam tape on the firewall and windscreen flanges.

Wing lift uses a Schrenk distribution, with each wing pinned at the cabin arch and a V-strut at the 2.4 m rib. Gust loads are below the manoeuvre case. Laminated spars are checked as one section, which assumes rivet pitch close enough to stop the layers buckling separately.
With X-ray on, every run is colour-coded: orange rudder, cyan elevator, purple aileron, green flap, red fuel, white pitot, grey static, yellow 12 V, pink coax.
With a helper at the tip, lift each wing until its root tangs slide into the arch-top clevises.

Yes, as a slow, gentle, lightly loaded single-seater: a strut-braced high wing, a half-VW engine and a tailwheel on big soft tyres. It is heavier than a typical ultralight because every aluminium part is cut from one gauge, with thicker parts made as nested folds of the same sheet. That puts it in UK SSDR (300 kg) rather than US Part 103. Every figure here comes from the same script that generates the cut files.
